zh: 胡光墉（1823—1885 ），字雪岩，安徽绩溪人。
en: Hu Guangyong (1823–1885), known by his courtesy name, Xueyan, was a native of Jixi, Anhui.

zh: 作者在书中极力铺陈了主人公的传奇经历，胡雪岩初在钱庄学徒，因囊助潦倒的冗吏王有龄旋升，以致自身失业，王有龄感其思，遂二人结生死之交。后胡雪岩利用王有龄在宫场上的发达，开设钱庄，在官府势力、漕帮首领和外商买办之间，层层投靠，左右逢源，以精细的连环计算，收买人民、网罗赌棍、拉拢富商，混迹于勾栏赌场，竭力经营丝茶生意，大做军火勾当。
en: In this novel, the author recounts his protagonist's extraordinary career in rich detail. Hu Xueyan begins as an apprentice in a private bank. After providing financial assistance that helps Wang Youling, an impoverished minor official, advance in his career, Hu loses his own job. Deeply grateful, Wang forms a bond with him that neither life nor death can break. Later, drawing on Wang's growing influence in official circles, Hu establishes his own bank. He cultivates patrons among government officials, leaders of the grain-transport associations, and Chinese intermediaries working for foreign merchants, building connections on every side. Through a succession of carefully calculated moves, he buys people's loyalty, recruits gamblers, and courts wealthy merchants. Frequenting brothels and gambling houses, he energetically develops his silk and tea businesses and engages extensively in the arms trade.

zh: 其问，收姬纳妾，邀友狎妓，不惜重金为妓女赎身，又转手奉送于高官……
en: Meanwhile, he acquires concubines, visits courtesans with his friends, and spends lavishly to buy women out of prostitution, only to present them in turn to high officials...

zh: 由于胡雪岩精于谋划，手段灵活，因此，很快得以暴发，终至在上海、杭州立足，由市井布衣，跻于江浙大贾之列。
en: An astute planner with flexible methods, Hu rapidly amasses a fortune. He establishes himself in Shanghai and Hangzhou, rising from the ranks of ordinary townspeople to become one of the great merchants of Jiangsu and Zhejiang.

zh: 列于《胡雪岩》（上、中、下）之后的《红顶商人》和《灯火楼台》等书（亦为台湾著名作家高阳先生所著，本公司出版），将继续向广大读者展现胡雪岩，这个半封建、半殖民地让会中的特定历史产物如何由商而宫、暴起暴落的曲折激烈的场面。
en: The Red-Topped Merchant and Towers of Light, which follow the three volumes of Hu Xueyan, are also by the celebrated Taiwan-based author Gao Yang and are published by our company. They continue the turbulent story of this figure shaped by a particular historical age: a semi-feudal, semi-colonial society. Readers will see how he moves from commerce into official life, and how his spectacular rise gives way to a dramatic fall.

zh: 在清朝咸丰七年，英商麦加利银行设分行于上海以前，全国金融事业，为两个集团所掌握，商业上的术语称为“帮”，北方是山西帮，南方地宁绍帮，所业虽同，其名则异，大致前者称为“票号”，后者称是“钱庄”。
en: Before the British Chartered Bank opened a branch in Shanghai in the seventh year of the Xianfeng reign, China's financial business was controlled by two groups, known in commercial usage as bang, or merchant networks. In the north stood the Shanxi network; in the south, the Ningbo–Shaoxing network. Although they pursued the same line of business, their establishments bore different names. Broadly speaking, those in the north were called piaohao, or remittance banks, while those in the south were known as qianzhuang, or private banks.

zh: 山西帮又分为祁、太，平三帮，祁县、太谷、平遥，而始创票号者，为平遥人雷履泰。他最初受雇于同县李姓，在天津主持一定颜料铺，招牌叫做“日升昌”，其时大约在乾隆末年。日升昌在雷履泰的悉心照料之下，营业日盛，声誉日起，连四川都知道这块“金字招牌”，因为雷履泰经常入川采购铜绿等等颜料，信用极好。
en: The Shanxi network was itself divided into three groups, based in Qixian, Taigu, and Pingyao. The founder of the remittance-bank business was Lei Lütai, a native of Pingyao. He had originally been employed by a man surnamed Li from the same county to manage a pigment shop in Tianjin called Rishengchang. This was around the end of the Qianlong reign. Under Lei's careful management, the business prospered and its reputation grew. Its name became a guarantee of quality known even in Sichuan, where Lei frequently purchased verdigris and other pigments and enjoyed an excellent reputation for reliability.

zh: 四川与他省的交通最不便，出川入川携带大批现金，不但麻烦，而且有风险。于是雷履泰创行汇兑法，由日升昌收银出票，凭票到指走地点的联号兑取现银。当然，汇兑要收汇费，名为“汇水”。汇水并无定额，是根据三个因素计算出来的：第一，路途的远近，远则贵，近则廉。第二，银根的松紧，大致由小地方汇到大地方来得便宜，由大地方汇到小地方来得贵，因为地方大则银根松，地方小则银根紧，如某处缺乏现金，而有待兑的汇票，则此时有客户交汇，正好济急，反有倒过来贴补客户汇费的。
en: Travel between Sichuan and the other provinces was particularly difficult. Carrying large amounts of cash into or out of the province was not only inconvenient but also dangerous. Lei therefore introduced a system of remittance: Rishengchang accepted silver and issued a draft that could be exchanged for silver at an affiliated establishment in a designated location. A remittance fee, known as huishui, was naturally charged. The fee was not fixed but depended on three factors. The first was distance: the farther the destination, the higher the charge. The second was the availability of ready money. As a rule, it cost less to remit funds from a small town to a large city than in the opposite direction, since ready money was more plentiful in larger places and scarcer in smaller ones. If a branch was short of cash and had outstanding drafts to redeem, a customer bringing in silver for remittance would provide much-needed relief. In such cases, the bank might even pay the customer a premium instead of charging a fee.

zh: 最后是计算银锭的成色，银锭的大小，通常分为三种，最大的五十两，为了便于双手携捧，做成两头翘起的马蹄式，即所谓“元宝”，而出于各省藩库的，称为“官宝”，其次是中锭，重十两，有元宝形的，称为“小元宝”，但通常都做成秤锤式，最小的或三两，或五两，通称“银锞”。再就是碎银，轻重不等。此外各省有其特殊的形制，如江浙称为“元丝”，底凹上凸，以便叠置。但不管任何形状、大小，银子的成色，各地不同，需要在交汇时核算扣足。
en: The final consideration was the purity of the silver ingots. Ingots generally came in three sizes. The largest weighed fifty taels and were shaped like a horseshoe with raised ends, making them easier to lift with both hands. These were the ingots known as yuanbao; those issued by provincial treasuries were called official ingots. Medium-sized ingots weighed ten taels. Some resembled the larger yuanbao and were called small yuanbao, though most were shaped like scale weights. The smallest weighed three or five taels and were commonly called silver lumps. There was also broken silver, which varied in weight. Each province had its own distinctive forms. In Jiangsu and Zhejiang, for example, the ingots known as yuansi had concave bases and convex tops so that they could be stacked. Whatever their shape or size, however, the purity of silver differed from place to place. These differences had to be calculated and fully allowed for when a remittance was made.

zh: 由于汇兑凭票兑银，所以叫做“票号”。早先运送现银的方法，如果不是随身携带，就得交镖局保送，费用大，麻烦多，走得慢，而且还有风险，万一被动或者出了其他意外，镖局虽然照赔，但总是件不愉快的事，所以票号一出，请教走镖英雄好汉的人就少了。
en: Since silver was paid out against a draft, these establishments came to be called piaohao, literally “draft houses.” Previously, anyone wishing to move silver had either to carry it personally or entrust it to an armed escort agency. The latter option was expensive, troublesome, and slow, and it still involved risk. If the silver was stolen or some other mishap occurred, the escort agency would reimburse the loss, but the experience was unpleasant nonetheless. Once remittance banks appeared, fewer people had occasion to seek the services of those valiant escorts.

zh: 早期的票号，多为大商号兼营的副业，到咸丰初年，始有大量专营的票号出现。但票号的势力不得越长江而南，因为江南的钱庄，为保护本身的利益，一方面仿照票号的成例，开办汇兑业务，一方面力拒票号的侵入。至于票号除汇兑以外，以后亦经营存款及放款，所以票号与钱庄的业务，由于彼此仿效的结果，几乎完全相同，只是在规模上，钱庄逊于票号而已。
en: The earliest remittance banks were mostly side businesses run by large trading firms. Only in the early years of the Xianfeng reign did establishments devoted exclusively to remittance begin to appear in considerable numbers. Their influence, however, did not extend south of the Yangtze. To protect their own interests, the private banks of the lower Yangtze region copied the remittance system while firmly resisting the northern banks' expansion. The remittance banks, in turn, later began accepting deposits and making loans. Through this process of mutual imitation, the two types of bank came to conduct almost identical business, although private banks generally remained smaller.

zh: 钱庄业多为宁绍帮所经营，而镇江帮有后来居上之势。但在同治到光绪初年，全国最大的一家钱庄，规模凌驾票号而上之，同时他的主人亦不属于宁绍帮，是为当时金融业中的一个特例。
en: Most private banks were operated by the Ningbo–Shaoxing network, though the Zhenjiang network was beginning to catch up and overtake it. Yet from the Tongzhi reign into the early years of Guangxu, the largest private bank in China surpassed even the remittance banks in scale. Its proprietor did not belong to the Ningbo–Shaoxing network either. It was an exception in the financial world of its time.

zh: 这家钱庄的字号叫“阜康”，它的主人是杭州人。
en: The bank was called Fukang. Its proprietor was a man from Hangzhou.

zh: 胡雪岩全传——平步青云（上）
en: The Complete Story of Hu Xueyan — A Swift Rise to Prominence, Volume I

zh: 有个福州人，名叫王有龄，他的父亲是候补道，分发浙江，在杭州一住数年，没有奉委过什么好差使。老病侵寻，心情抑郁，死在异乡。身后没有留下多少钱，运灵柩回福州，要好一笔盘缠，而且家乡也没有什么可以倚靠的亲友，王有龄就只好奉母寄居在异地了。
en: There was a man from Fuzhou named Wang Youling. His father, an expectant circuit intendant assigned to Zhejiang, had lived in Hangzhou for several years without receiving any worthwhile appointment. Worn down by age and illness, and burdened by disappointment, he died far from home. He left little money. Transporting his coffin back to Fuzhou would have cost a substantial sum, and there were no relatives or friends in their home town on whom the family could rely. Wang Youling therefore had little choice but to remain in Hangzhou with his mother.

zh: 境况不好，而且举目无亲，王有龄混得很不成样子，每天在“梅花碑”一家茶店里穷泡，一壶“龙井”泡成白开水还舍不得走，中午四个制钱买两个烧饼，算是一顿。
en: Short of money and with no one to turn to, Wang lived in miserable circumstances. He spent his days lingering in a teahouse at Meihuabei, reluctant to leave even after his pot of Longjing tea had been brewed until it tasted like plain water. At noon he spent four copper coins on two baked flatbreads and called that a meal.

zh: 三十岁的人，潦倒落拓，无精打采，叫人看了起反感。他的架子还大，经常两眼朝天，那就越发没有人爱理他了。
en: At thirty, he was shabby, dispirited, and down on his luck—a sight that put people off. Yet he still gave himself airs, often looking down his nose at everyone, which made them even less inclined to have anything to do with him.

zh: 唯一的例外是个二十岁左右的少年，王有龄只知道他叫“小胡”。小胡生得一双四面八方都照顾得到的眼睛，加上一张常开的笑口，而且为人“四海”，所以人缘极好。不过，王有龄跟他只是点头之交，也识不透他的身分，有时很阔气，有时似乎很窘，但不管如何，总是衣衫光鲜，象这初夏的天气，一件细白夏布长衫，浆洗得极其挺括，里面是纺绸小褂裤，脚上白竹布的袜子，玄色贡缎的双梁鞋，跟王有龄身上那件打过补钉的青布长衫一比，小胡真可以说是“公子哥儿”了。
en: The sole exception was a young man of about twenty, whom Wang knew only as Young Hu. He had eyes that seemed to take in everything around him, a ready smile, and an easy generosity that made him welcome wherever he went. Wang, however, knew him only well enough to exchange a nod and could not make out his circumstances. At times he seemed well supplied with money; at others, decidedly short of it. Whatever his fortunes, he was always neatly dressed. In this early-summer weather, for instance, he wore a fine white ramie gown, washed and starched until it was beautifully crisp, over a short silk jacket and silk trousers. His socks were of white cotton, and his black satin shoes had twin raised seams. Beside Wang's patched blue cotton gown, Young Hu's appearance was positively that of a wealthy young gentleman.

zh: 他倒是有意结交王有龄，王有龄却以自惭形秽，淡淡地不肯跟他接近。
en: Young Hu clearly wished to make friends with Wang, but Wang felt ashamed of his own poverty and kept him at a distance.

zh: 这一天下午的茶客特别多，小胡跟王有龄“拼桌”，他去下了两盘象棋，笑嘻嘻走回来说：“王有龄，走，走，我请你去‘摆一碗’。”摆一碗是杭州的乡谈，意思是到小酒店去对酌一番。
en: One afternoon the teahouse was unusually crowded, and the two shared a table. Young Hu went off to play a couple of games of Chinese chess. When he returned, he was beaming. “Wang Youling, come along! Let me buy you a drink.” His expression, “set out a bowl,” was a Hangzhou phrase for going to a little tavern to share some wine.

zh: “谢谢。不必破费。”
en: “Thank you, but you needn't go to the expense.”

zh: “自有人请客。你看！”他打开手巾包，里面包有二两碎银子，得意地笑道：“第一盘‘双车错’，第二盘‘马后炮’，第三盘，小卒‘逼宫’，杀得路断人稀。不然，我还要赢。”
en: “Someone else is paying. Look!” He opened a bundle wrapped in a handkerchief to reveal two taels of broken silver. Grinning proudly, he said, “In the first game I caught him with a pair of chariots; in the second, with a cannon behind a horse. In the third, a little pawn cornered his general. I routed them so thoroughly that there was no one left to play. Otherwise, I'd have won still more.”

zh: 为了盛情难却，王有龄跟着去了。一路走到“城隍山”——“立马吴山第一峰”的吴山，挑了个可以眺望万家灯火的空旷地方，一面喝酒一面闲谈。
en: Unable to resist such a warm invitation, Wang went along. They walked to City God Hill—the Wushan celebrated in the line, “Rein in your horse upon Wushan's foremost peak”—and chose an open spot overlooking the lights of countless homes. There they drank and talked.

zh: 酒到半酣，闲话也说得差不多了，小胡忽然提高了声音说：“王有龄，我有句话，老早想问你了。我看你不是没本事的人，而且我也懂点‘麻衣相法’，看你是大贵之相，何以一天到晚‘孵’茶店？”
en: When the wine had begun to take effect and their small talk was nearly exhausted, Young Hu suddenly raised his voice. “Wang Youling, there's something I've been wanting to ask you for a long time. You don't strike me as a man without ability. I also know a little of the Mayi art of face-reading, and yours looks like the face of a man destined for high office. Why do you spend all day nesting in a teahouse?”

zh: 王有龄摇摇头，拈了块城隍山上有名的油饼，慢慢咬着，双眼望着远处，是那种说不出来的茫然落寞。
en: Wang shook his head. He picked up one of the fried cakes for which City God Hill was famous and ate it slowly, gazing into the distance with an expression of bewildered loneliness that was hard to put into words.

zh: “叫我说什么？”王有龄转过脸来盯着小胡，仿佛要跟他吵架似的，“做生意要本钱，做官也要本钱，没本钱说什么？”
en: “What am I supposed to say?” He turned and stared at Young Hu as though about to quarrel with him. “It takes capital to go into business, and it takes capital to become an official. Without capital, what's there to talk about?”

zh: “做官？”小胡大为诧异，“怎么做法？你同我一样，连‘学’都没有‘进’过，是个白丁。哪里来的官做？”
en: “Become an official?” Young Hu was astonished. “How would you manage that? You're like me: you've never even earned the first examination qualification. We're ordinary men without degrees. Where would an official post come from?”

zh: “不可以‘捐班’吗？”
en: “Couldn't I enter by purchasing a qualification?”

zh: 小胡默然。心里有些看不起王有龄。捐官的情形不外乎两种，一种是做生意发了财，富而不贵，美中不足，捐个功名好提高身价，象扬州的盐商，个个都是花几千两银子捐来的道台，那一来便可以与地方官称兄道弟，平起平坐，否则就不算“缙绅先生”，育事上得公堂，要跪着回话。再有一种，本是官员家的子弟，书也读得不错，就是运气不好，三年大比，次次名落孙山，年纪大了，家计也艰窘了，总得想个谋生之道，走的就是“做官”的这条路，改行也无从改起，只好卖田卖地，拜托亲友，凑一笔去捐个官做。象王有龄这样，年纪还轻，应该刻苦用功，从正途上去巴结，不此之图，而况又穷得衣食不周，却痴心妄想去捐班，岂不是没出息？
en: Young Hu said nothing, but inwardly he thought rather less of Wang. There were generally two kinds of people who bought official status. One was the merchant who had made his fortune but felt that wealth without rank left something to be desired. He bought a title to raise his standing. The salt merchants of Yangzhou, for example, had each spent several thousand taels to acquire the rank of circuit intendant. That enabled them to address local officials as brothers and meet them as equals. Without such standing, they did not count as members of the gentry and had to kneel when answering questions in court. The other kind was the son of an official: well educated, perhaps, but unlucky enough to fail the examinations every three years. As he grew older and his family resources dwindled, he had to find a way to earn a living. Official service was the only career for which he had been prepared; he could scarcely begin again in another trade. So he sold fields and property, sought help from relatives and friends, and scraped together enough money to buy a qualification. Wang Youling, however, was still young. Surely he ought to study hard and work his way up through the regular examinations. Instead, though he could barely feed and clothe himself, he was dreaming of buying his way into office. Did that not show a lack of ambition?

zh: 王有龄看出他心里的意思，有几杯酒在肚里，便不似平时那么沉着了，“小胡！”他说，“我告诉你一句话，信不信由你，先父在日，替我捐过一个‘盐大使’。”
en: Wang guessed what he was thinking. With several cups of wine inside him, he was less restrained than usual. “Young Hu,” he said, “I'll tell you something, whether you believe it or not. While my father was alive, he bought me a qualification as a salt-station superintendent.”

zh: 小胡最机警，一看他的神情，就知道决非假话，随即笑道：“唷！失敬，失敬，原来是王老爷，一直连名带姓叫你，不知者不罪。”
en: Young Hu was exceptionally quick-witted. One look at Wang's expression told him this was no invention. He immediately smiled. “Oh! My apologies! So you are His Honour Wang. And all this time I've been calling you by your full name. You must forgive an ignorant man.”

zh: “不要挖苦我了！”王有龄苦笑道，“说句实话，除非是你，别人面前我再也不说，说了反惹人耻笑。”
en: “Don't make fun of me.” Wang smiled bitterly. “To tell the truth, you're the only person I'd say this to. Anyone else would only laugh.”

zh: “我不是笑你。”小胡放出庄重的神态问道，“不过，有一层我不明白，既然你是盐大使，我们浙江沿海有好几十个盐场，为什么不给你补缺？”
en: “I'm not laughing at you.” Young Hu grew serious. “But there's one thing I don't understand. If you're qualified to be a salt-station superintendent, why haven't you been appointed? There must be dozens of saltworks along the Zhejiang coast.”

zh: “你只知其一，不知其二……”
en: “You know only half the story...”

zh: 捐官只是捐一个虚衔，凭一张吏部所发的“执照”，取得某一类官员的资格，如果要想补缺，必得到吏部报到，称为“投供”，然后抽签分发到某一省候补。王有龄尚未“投供”，哪里谈得到补缺？
en: Purchasing office meant, in the first instance, purchasing an empty title. A certificate issued by the Board of Civil Appointments made its holder eligible for a particular category of post. To obtain an actual appointment, he first had to report to the Board for registration and then draw lots for assignment to a province, where he would wait for a vacancy. Wang had not even completed the registration. How could he expect a substantive post?

zh: 讲完这些捐官补缺的程序，王有龄又说：“我所说的要‘本钱’，就是进京投供的盘缠。如果境况再宽裕些，我还想‘改捐’。”
en: After explaining the procedure, Wang added, “The ‘capital’ I mean is the money to travel to the capital and register. If I had a little more to spare, I'd also like to purchase a different qualification.”

zh: “改捐个什么‘班子’？”
en: “For what sort of post?”

zh: “改捐个知县。盐大使正八品，知县正七品，改捐花不了多少钱。出路可就大不相同了。”
en: “A county magistracy. A salt-station superintendent holds the principal eighth rank; a county magistrate holds the principal seventh. Changing qualifications wouldn't cost very much, but the prospects would be entirely different.”

zh: “怎么呢？”
en: “How so?”

zh: “盐大使只管盐场，出息倒也不错，不过没有意思。知县虽小，一县的父母官，能杀人也能活人，可以好好做一番事业。”
en: “A salt-station superintendent manages a saltworks, nothing more. The income can be quite good, but the work has little meaning. A county magistrate may be a minor official, yet he is responsible for the welfare of an entire county. He has the power to take lives or save them. He can accomplish something worthwhile.”

zh: 这两句话使得小胡肃然起敬，把刚才看不起他的那点感想，一扫而空了。
en: These words filled Young Hu with respect, sweeping away every trace of his earlier contempt.

zh: “再说，知县到底是正印官，不比盐大使，说起来总是佐杂，又是捐班的佐杂，到处做‘磕头虫’，与我的性情也不相宜。”
en: “Besides, a county magistrate is the chief official of his jurisdiction. A salt-station superintendent is only a subordinate, and one who has purchased his qualification at that. He has to bow and scrape wherever he goes. That doesn't suit my temperament.”

zh: “对，对！”小胡不断点头，“那么，这一来，你要多少‘本钱’才够呢？”
en: “Quite right!” Young Hu nodded repeatedly. “Then how much ‘capital’ would you need?”

zh: “总得五百两银子。”
en: “At least five hundred taels of silver.”

zh: “噢！”小胡没有再接口，王有龄也不再提，五百两银子不是小数目，小胡不见得会有，就有也不见得肯借。
en: “Oh.” Young Hu said no more, and Wang let the subject drop. Five hundred taels was no small sum. Young Hu might not possess it; even if he did, he might not be willing to lend it.

zh: 两人各有心事，吃闷酒无味，天也黑上来了，王有龄推杯告辞，小胡也不留他，只说：“明天下午，我仍旧在这里等你，你来！”
en: Each was now absorbed in his own thoughts. Drinking in silence had lost its charm, and darkness was gathering. Wang pushed his cup away and rose to leave. Young Hu did not try to detain him. He merely said, “I'll be here again tomorrow afternoon. Come and meet me.”

zh: “有事吗？”王有龄微感诧异，“何不此刻就说？”
en: “Is there something you want?” Wang asked, slightly surprised. “Why not tell me now?”

zh: “我有点小事托你，此刻还没有想停当。还是明天下午再谈。你一定要来，我在这里坐等，不见不散。”
en: “There's a small favour I'd like to ask, but I haven't quite thought it through. Let's talk tomorrow afternoon. You must come. I'll wait here until you do.”

zh: 看他如此叮嘱，王有龄也就答应了。到了第二天下午，依约而至，不见小胡的踪影。泡一碗茶得好几文钱，对王有龄来说，是一种浪费，于是沿着山路一直走了过去。城隍山上有好几座庙，庙前有耍把戏的，打拳卖膏药的，摆象棋摊的，不花钱而可以消磨时光的地方多得很。他这里立一会，那面看一看，到红日衔山，方始走回原处，依旧不见小胡。
en: Young Hu was so insistent that Wang agreed. The next afternoon he arrived as promised, but there was no sign of his young acquaintance. A bowl of tea cost several copper coins, which Wang considered an unnecessary extravagance, so he continued along the hillside path. There were several temples on City God Hill. Before their gates stood acrobats, performers demonstrating martial arts to sell their medicinal plasters, and men with chessboards set up for challengers. There were plenty of ways to pass the time without spending money. Wang stopped here and watched there, returning to the meeting place only when the red sun touched the hills. Young Hu was still nowhere to be seen.

zh: 是“不见不散”的死约会。王有龄顿感进退两难，不等是自己失约，要等，天色已暮，晚饭尚无着落。呆了半天，越想越急，顿一顿足，往山下便走，心中自语：明天见着小胡，非说他几句不可！他又不是不知道自己的境况，在外面吃碗茶都得先算一算，何苦捉弄人？
en: They had expressly agreed to wait until they met. Wang found himself in a quandary. If he left, he would be breaking his word; if he stayed, night would soon fall, and he had made no provision for supper. He stood there for some time, growing more anxious with every thought. Finally, he stamped his foot and started downhill. Tomorrow, he told himself, he would certainly give Young Hu a piece of his mind. The young fellow knew perfectly well how things stood with him: even a bowl of tea away from home had to be carefully considered. Why torment him like this?

zh: 走了不多几步，听见后面有人在叫：“王有龄，王有龄！”
en: He had gone only a few steps when someone called from behind, “Wang Youling! Wang Youling!”

zh: 转身一看，正是小胡，手里拿着手巾包，跑得气喘吁吁，满脸是汗。见着了他的面，王有龄的气消了一半，问道：“你怎么这时候才来？”
en: He turned to see Young Hu running towards him, a handkerchief bundle in his hand, breathless and drenched in sweat. Half of Wang's anger vanished at the sight. “Why are you only arriving now?” he asked.

zh: “我知道你等得久了，对不起，对不起！”小胡欣慰地笑着，“总算还好，耽迟不耽错。来，来，坐下来再说。”
en: “I know you've been waiting a long time. I'm sorry, truly sorry.” Young Hu smiled with relief. “Still, all's well. I'm late, but I haven't missed you. Come, let's sit down and talk.”

zh: 王有龄也不知道他这话是什么意思？默默地跟着他走向一副设在橱下的座头，泡了两碗茶。小胡有些魂不守舍似的，目送着经过的行人，手里紧捏住那个手巾包。
en: Wang had no idea what he meant. He followed silently to a table beneath the eaves, where they ordered two bowls of tea. Young Hu seemed distracted. He watched the passers-by while gripping the handkerchief bundle tightly.

zh: “小胡！”王有龄忍不住问了：“你说有事托我，快说吧！”
en: “Young Hu!” Wang could contain himself no longer. “You said you wanted a favour. What is it?”

zh: “你打开来看，不要给人看见。”他低声地说，把手巾包递了给王有龄。
en: “Open this and look. Don't let anyone see,” he whispered, handing over the bundle.

zh: 他避开行人，悄悄启视，里面是一叠银票，还有些碎银子，约莫有十几两。
en: Shielding it from passing eyes, Wang opened it discreetly. Inside was a stack of bank drafts and some broken silver, perhaps a little over ten taels.

zh: “怎么回事？”
en: “What's all this?”

zh: “这就是你做官的本钱。”
en: “The capital you need to become an official.”

zh: 王有龄愣住了，一下子心里发酸，眼眶发热，尽力忍住眼泪，把手巾包放在桌上，却不知怎么说才好。
en: Wang was stunned. His heart suddenly ached and his eyes grew hot. Fighting back tears, he put the bundle on the table, unable to find a word to say.

zh: “你最好点一点数。其中有一张三百两的，是京城里‘大德恒’的票子，认票不认人，你要当心失落。另外我又替你换了些零碎票子，都是有名的‘字号’，一路上通行无阻。”小胡又说：“如果不为换票子，我早就来了。”
en: “You'd better count it. One draft is for three hundred taels, issued by Dadeheng in the capital. It's payable to whoever presents it, so be careful not to lose it. I've also changed some of the money into smaller drafts, all from well-known firms. You'll be able to use them all along the way.” Young Hu added, “If it hadn't taken so long to change the drafts, I'd have been here much earlier.”

zh: 这里王有龄才想出来一句话：“小胡，你为什么待我这么好？”
en: Only then did Wang find something to say. “Young Hu, why are you so good to me?”

zh: “朋友嘛！”小胡答道，“我看你好比虎落平阳，英雄末路，心里说不出的难过，一定要拉你一把，才睡得着觉。”
en: “Because we're friends!” Young Hu replied. “Seeing you like this—a tiger stranded on the plain, a hero with nowhere to turn—makes me more miserable than I can say. I couldn't sleep unless I gave you a hand.”

zh: “唉！”王有龄毕竟忍不住了，两行热泪，牵连不断。
en: “Ah!” Wang could hold back no longer. Tears streamed down his face.

zh: “何必，何必？这不是大丈夫气概！”
en: “Come now, come now! Where's your courage?”

zh: 这句话是很好的安慰，也是很好的激励、王有龄收拾涕泪，定一定神，才想起一件事，相交至今，受人绝大的恩惠，却是对他的名氏、身世，一无所知，岂不荒唐？
en: The words comforted him and restored his spirits. Wang wiped his tears away and composed himself. Only then did something occur to him: he had received an immense kindness from a man whose full name and background he did not even know. How absurd!

zh: 于是他微有窘色地问道：“小胡，还没有请教台甫？”
en: Slightly embarrassed, he asked, “Young Hu, I haven't yet had the honour of learning your courtesy name.”

zh: “我叫胡光墉，字雪岩，你呢，你的大号叫什么？”
en: “My name is Hu Guangyong, and my courtesy name is Xueyan. What about yours?”

zh: “我叫雪轩。”
en: “Xuexuan.”

zh: “雪轩，雪岩！”胡雪岩自己念了两遍，抚掌笑道：“好极了，声音很近，好象一个人。你叫我雪岩，我叫你雪轩。”
en: “Xuexuan, Xueyan!” Hu repeated the names twice, then clapped his hands and laughed. “Splendid! They sound so alike we might almost be the same person. You call me Xueyan, and I'll call you Xuexuan.”

zh: “是，是！雪岩，我还要请教你，府上……”
en: “Yes, yes! Xueyan, there's something else I'd like to ask. Your family...”

zh: 这是问他的家世，胡雪岩笑笑不肯多说：“守一点薄产过日了，没有什么谈头。雪轩，我问你，你几时动身？”
en: He was asking about Hu's background, but Hu merely smiled and declined to say much. “I live on a little property. There's nothing worth mentioning. Tell me, Xuexuan, when will you leave?”

zh: “我不敢耽搁。把舍间咯略安排一番，总在三、五日内就动身。如果一切顺利，年底就可以回来。雪岩，我一定要走路子，分发到浙江来，你我弟兄好在一起。”
en: “I dare not delay. Once I've put things in order at home, I'll set off within three to five days. If all goes well, I should be back by the end of the year. Xueyan, I'll do everything I can to secure an assignment to Zhejiang, so that we two brothers can be together.”

zh: “好极了。”胡雪岩的“好极了”，已成口头禅，“后天我们仍旧在这里会面，我给你饯行。”
en: “Splendid!” The word was already becoming Hu's habitual response. “Let's meet here again the day after tomorrow. I'll give you a farewell dinner.”

zh: “我一定来。”
en: “I'll certainly come.”

zh: 到了第三天，王有龄午饭刚过，就来赴约。他穿了估衣铺买的直罗长衫，亮纱马褂，手里拿一柄“舒莲记”有名的“杭扇”，泡着茶等，等到夭黑不见胡雪岩的踪影，寻亦没处寻，只好再等。
en: On the appointed day, Wang came just after lunch. He wore a gauze gown and a glossy gauze riding jacket bought at a second-hand clothes shop, and carried one of the famous Hangzhou folding fans made by Shulianji. He ordered tea and waited. Darkness fell without any sign of Hu. There was nowhere he could go to look for him, so he could only keep waiting.

zh: 天气热了，城隍山上来品茗纳凉的，络绎不绝。王有龄目迎目送着每一个行人，把脖子都摆得酸了，就是盼不着胡雪岩。
en: The weather had grown hot, and a steady stream of people came up City God Hill to drink tea and enjoy the cool air. Wang watched every arrival and departure until his neck ached, but the man he hoped to see never appeared.

zh: 夜深客散，茶店收摊子，这下才把王有龄撵走。他已经雇好了船，无法不定，第二天五更时分上船，竟不能与胡雪岩见一面话别。
en: Late at night, when the customers had gone and the teahouse was closing, Wang finally had to leave. He had already hired a boat and could not cancel his departure. He boarded in the hours before dawn the next morning, without having had a chance to see Hu and say goodbye.

zh: 在王有龄北上不久，浙江的政局有了变化：巡抚常大淳调湖北，云南巡抚黄宗汉改调浙江，未到任以前由布政使——通称“藩司”、老百姓尊称为“藩台”的旗人椿寿署理。
en: Shortly after Wang left for the north, Zhejiang's provincial administration changed. Governor Chang Dachun was transferred to Hubei, and Huang Zonghan, governor of Yunnan, was reassigned to Zhejiang. Until Huang arrived, the acting governorship was held by Chunshou, a bannerman serving as provincial treasurer—a post commonly called fansi and respectfully referred to by ordinary people as fantai.

zh: 黄宗汉字寿臣，福建晋江人。他是道光十五年乙未正科的翰林，这一榜人才济济，科运甚隆，那年，咸丰二年，当到巡抚的就有三个，广东叶名琛、江西张芾，当到二品大员的有何桂清、吕贤基、彭蕴章、罗惇衍，还有杭州的许乃钊，与他老兄许乃普，都当内阁学士。
en: Huang Zonghan, whose courtesy name was Shouchen, came from Jinjiang in Fujian. He had entered the Hanlin Academy after passing the regular metropolitan examination in the fifteenth year of the Daoguang reign, the yiwei year. That examination produced a remarkable crop of talented men whose careers prospered. By the year in question, the second year of Xianfeng, three had become provincial governors: Huang himself, Ye Mingchen in Guangdong, and Zhang Fu in Jiangxi. Others who had reached the second official rank included He Guiqing, Lü Xianji, Peng Yunzhang, and Luo Dunyan. Xu Naizhao of Hangzhou and his elder brother Xu Naipu had both become grand secretariat academicians.

zh: 这黄宗汉据说是个很能干的人，但是关于他的操守与治家，批评极坏。
en: Huang was said to be highly capable, but his personal integrity and the management of his household were subjects of severe criticism.

zh: 到任以后，传说他向椿寿索贿四万两银子，椿寿没有买他的帐，于是多事了。
en: After taking office, he was said to have demanded a bribe of forty thousand taels from Chunshou. Chunshou ignored the demand, and trouble followed.

zh: 其时漕运正在改变办法。因为海禁已开，而且河道湮淤，加以洪杨的起事，所以江苏的苏、松、太各属改用海运，浙江则是试办，椿寿既为藩司，又署理巡抚，责无旁贷，当然要亲自料理这件公事。
en: At the time, the system for transporting the grain tax was undergoing change. Maritime restrictions had been lifted, river channels were silting up, and the rebellion led by Hong Xiuquan and Yang Xiuqing had broken out. The jurisdictions of Suzhou, Songjiang, and Taicang in Jiangsu therefore switched to sea transport, while Zhejiang was preparing to try it. As both provincial treasurer and acting governor, Chunshou could not evade responsibility. He had to oversee the matter personally.

zh: 漕运的漕，原来就是以舟运谷的意思。多少年来都是河运，先是黄河，后来是运河，而运河又有多少次的变迁兴作，直到康熙年间，治河名臣靳辅，于成龙先后开“中河”，历时千余年的运河，才算大功告成。
en: The word cao in caoyun, the grain-tax transport system, originally meant carrying grain by boat. For centuries the grain had travelled by river, first on the Yellow River and later on the Grand Canal. The canal itself had undergone repeated changes and construction. Only during the Kangxi reign, when the celebrated river administrators Jin Fu and Yu Chenglong successively opened sections of the Middle Canal, was this waterway, more than a thousand years in the making, finally considered complete.

zh: 这条南起杭州，北抵京师，流经浙江、江苏、山东、河北四省，全长两千多里的水道，为大清朝带来了一百五十年的盛运。不幸的是，黄河的情况，越来越坏，有些地方，河底积淤，高过人家屋脊，全靠两面堤防约束，“春水船如天上行”，真到了束手无策的地步。而运河受黄河的累，在嘉庆末年，几乎也成了“绝症”。于是道光初年有海运之议。
en: Running from Hangzhou in the south to the capital in the north, through Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Shandong, and Hebei, the waterway extended for more than two thousand li and had brought the Qing dynasty a century and a half of prosperity. Unfortunately, conditions on the Yellow River grew steadily worse. In places, accumulated silt raised its bed above the rooftops of nearby houses, leaving the river confined only by the embankments on either side. “On spring waters, boats seem to sail through the sky”: matters had truly reached the point where no remedy seemed possible. Burdened by the Yellow River's troubles, the Grand Canal itself was almost beyond cure by the end of the Jiaqing reign. Hence the proposal, early in the Daoguang reign, to ship the grain by sea.
